paras: The threatened lynching of Charles Merrill took place on February 27, 1881, in China, Kennebec County, Maine, when a crowd of local people threatened Merrill, a young man held by a deputy sheriff on the charge of murdering his mother. Officers took him to the jail at Augusta that day for fear of an attempt to lynch him after dark, and he was later convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment. Papers treated the killing itself as the most atrocious murder in the state's history and mentioned the threat as a side detail.

Deborah Merrill, 54, lived with her son Charles, nearly 23, in half of a farmhouse about a mile north of Week's Mills, while her daughter, Mrs. Lilly, lived in the other half. According to the Kennebec Journal, the son had been arrested several times for stealing and had been turned out of the house the previous fall after voting the Greenback ticket. Neighbors last saw the mother alive about February 18 or 19, and after several days her daughter's suspicions led to a search directed by Deputy Sheriff Frank Percival.

On Saturday, February 26, searchers found burned human remains in the manure heap and around the house, and Percival arrested Merrill and kept him overnight at Week's Mills. By the Kennebec Journal's account, "hundreds of country people" had gathered around the farmhouse in "intense excitement" by the time Coroner Libby arrived on Sunday morning. When physicians pronounced the remains human, the crowd surged against the door "muttering imprecations and threats," and the paper noted that no constable was present.

Merrill confessed that day to Libby and Percival. He was then taken straight to Augusta because, the Journal wrote, officers feared that "an attempt would be made to lynch him as soon as darkness set in." On the way he showed officers where he had buried the trunk of the body in the snow, and he was held in the Augusta jail. No attempt on him is described in the coverage.

No arrests of crowd members were reported. Merrill's trial opened at Augusta on May 10, 1881, where his counsel conceded the homicide and argued that it was manslaughter committed in a struggle in the stable. The jury returned a verdict of first-degree murder in six minutes, and Judge Whitehouse sentenced him to hard labor in the State Prison for life.

Maine papers covered the case at length, with the Kennebec Journal headlining it "One of the Most Atrocious Murders in the Annals of Crime!" A Republican Journal correspondent in China wrote that neighbors would "doubtless" have lynched Merrill had they learned of his confession before he left for Augusta. The Ellsworth American reported "considerable talk of lynching" but judged there was little danger of it among "the law-abiding people of Maine," and used the case to argue for restoring capital punishment.

Outside Maine, an Augusta dispatch dated February 27 said he "narrowly escaped lynching," as printed in the Chicago Daily Tribune and the Kentucky Gazette. A syndicated "News Epitome" paragraph, which put the crowd at 500 and said it "threatened to lynch him," ran in New Jersey, Rhode Island and South Carolina papers through mid-March. None of the papers mentioned anyone's race.

Accounts differ on how close the crowd came to acting, from talk of lynching and threats at the door in the Maine papers to a narrow escape in the wire version. The crowd was "hundreds" in the on-scene Kennebec Journal report and 500 in the epitome, and one wire dated the killing Friday the 18th where local reports and the trial gave Saturday the 19th.

bases: A crowd at China threatened a man held by a deputy sheriff on a murder charge, and officers moved him to the Augusta jail for fear of a lynching (A2, A3, A9); nothing in the coverage indicates the accused or the crowd was Black.

No one was killed: Merrill was removed to the Augusta jail, later tried and sentenced to life (A3, A14). The threat came from a crowd of 'hundreds' or 500 with no lawful authority, angered by the murder charge (A2, A9), so this was a threatened lynching only.

The local Kennebec Journal (A2, A3), a Republican Journal correspondent in China (A7), the Ellsworth American (A8) and the wire and epitome versions (A6, A9) independently report the lynching threat, though they differ on how close it came.

framing.detail: The Kennebec Journal ('HORRRIBLE', 'One of the Most Atrocious Murders in the Annals of Crime!') centered the crime and described the crowd's anger without comment.
The Ellsworth American doubted Maine people would lynch but said the tendency arose because the crime would not be 'suitably punished', using the case to argue for restoring capital punishment.
Out-of-state papers ran the wire ('A Fiend Murders His Mother') and a 'News Epitome' paragraph from Kentucky to New Jersey, Rhode Island and South Carolina.

info: Crowd gathered and threatened Merrill on Sunday, Feb. 27, 1881; he was taken to Augusta that day after confessing. The killing of his mother was dated Saturday, Feb. 19 in local reports and at trial (one wire says Friday the 18th).
The Merrill farmhouse about a mile north of Week's Mills, in the town of China, about twelve miles from Augusta; Merrill was held at Deputy Sheriff Percival's residence/store at Week's Mills.
Charles Merrill (Charles E. Merrill), about 23 (25 in one account), threatened, not harmed. Race not stated.
Accused of murdering his mother, Mrs. Deborah Merrill, 54, with a hammer and dismembering and burning her body; he was reported to have confessed.
Neighbors and country people of China gathered at the Merrill house; not named.
Convicted of first-degree murder after six minutes' deliberation and sentenced to hard labor in the State Prison for life.
